title: Visualising Entrepreneurs, Business Size and Integration

visual_beats.directive: Draw the founder and three delivery vans
Pop five trait panels around the portrait
Merge the trait panels into an enterprise badge

narration.text: An entrepreneur organises resources, takes risks and makes decisions in the hope of profit. Soffia Khan founded Northbeam Couriers with three vans. Successful entrepreneurs show resilience when deliveries fail, creativity in new routes, confidence, determination and the ability to communicate with drivers. Because she combined land, labour and capital, she created a business. Therefore enterprise is the organising, risk-taking factor of production.

scenes.title: The Business Plan as a Road Map

visual_beats.directive: Open the document and unfold eight section tabs
Highlight finance forecasts and market research
Send a route line from the plan to a launched van

narration.text: Soffia wrote a business plan before launching. It contains an overview or summary, clear objectives, the resources needed, market research, a marketing strategy, operations, finance forecasts and the people required. A plan helps secure finance. It forces the owner to test assumptions before launch. Because the plan reveals weak demand early, therefore the business can change course. So a written plan reduces risk and guides decisions.

scenes.title: How Do We Measure Business Size?
labels: Value or volume of output and sales
Profit is not a size measure

visual_beats.directive: Bring up each meter with its own scale
Strike through the profit meter
Show two meters disagreeing to prove no single measure is perfect

narration.text: Business size can be measured by the number of people employed, the value or volume of output and sales, or capital employed. Profit is not a method of measuring business size. Northbeam Couriers can be large by staff count but small by sales value, while a specialist firm may show the reverse. Because no single measure is perfect, therefore exam answers should compare at least two.

visual_beats.directive: Run the employee counter from forty to one hundred twenty
Grow the revenue bar from 1.2 to 3.8 million dollars
Raise the capital employed counter from 0.4 to 1.1 million

narration.text: Let's measure Northbeam Couriers. At launch it employed forty people and generated one point two million dollars of sales revenue. After expansion it employed one hundred twenty people and reached three point eight million dollars of sales. Capital employed rose from four hundred thousand to one point one million dollars. The employee counter shows growth; the revenue bar shows a bigger jump. Value added rose too.

scenes.title: Organic Growth: New Products and Markets

visual_beats.directive: Reveal the existing delivery network
Add a new product node and a new city node
Animate added value coins funding extra vans

narration.text: Growth can be internal, also called organic growth. Northbeam Couriers develops new products, such as refrigerated delivery, and new markets, such as a neighbouring city. Because the firm uses its own resources and existing staff, therefore it grows gradually and keeps control. So risk stays lower than a takeover, although expansion is slower. The added value earned from each delivery provides funds for many more vans and trained drivers.

scenes.title: External Growth: Horizontal Integration
labels: Northbeam Couriers plus Pinnacle Parcel Works

visual_beats.directive: Show two separate courier company blocks
Slide them together along a merge path
Display the larger combined block with market share rising

narration.text: External growth happens through a merger or takeover. Northbeam Couriers merges with Pinnacle Parcel Works, another courier firm at the same stage of production. That is horizontal integration. The two company blocks slide together and form one larger block. Alternatively, a takeover occurs when one business buys another. Because the combined firm serves more customers and routes, therefore it gains market share and bargaining power.

scenes.title: Vertical Integration and the Trade-Off
labels: Backward: buy supplier Vertex Van Bodies
Benefit: supply control and customer access
Cost: poor communication, loss of control

visual_beats.directive: Highlight the upstream supplier block then the downstream partner
Fill the left benefit panel with control icons
Fill the right limitation panel with warning icons

narration.text: Vertical integration joins firms at different stages of the same industry. Northbeam Couriers buys Vertex Van Bodies, a supplier, for backward integration. Later it links with Doorstep Direct, a delivery network closer to customers, for forward integration. On one side, this gives control of supply and access to customers. On the other side, the firm may lack manufacturing skill, and growth can bring poor communication and loss of control. Therefore managers must weigh control against complexity.

visual_beats.directive: Show the van maker block joining from upstream
Light the backward vertical integration option
Bring up two size meters and cross out profit

narration.text: Final check. Northbeam Couriers buys Vertex Van Bodies, which makes the vans it uses. Is that horizontal or vertical integration, and which direction? Buying a supplier is backward vertical integration, because the supplier is at an earlier stage of production. Horizontal integration would mean buying another courier firm. Name two valid measures of business size, and explain why profit is not one. Watch the blocks move into place as you answer.

recap_quiz.question: Northbeam Couriers buys Vertex Van Bodies, the company that builds its delivery vans. What type of integration is this?
recap_quiz.visual_explanation: A van-body factory block sits upstream of the courier block, an animated path connects them, and the factory block slides into the courier firm while a backward vertical integration label appears.
